papers.title: Maintaining EHR-based Predictive Clinical Decision Support in Mental Health against Temporal Shifts
papers.abstract: Electronic health record (EHR)-based risk prediction offers opportunities for early intervention in mental health, but models may remain in use as patient populations, care practices, and documentation change. Such temporal shifts can reduce predictive performance, while updating models from recent data alone may be unstable when adverse outcomes are uncommon. We developed Adversarial Drift-Aware Predictive Transfer (ADAPT), a distributionally robust approach to improve the temporal durability of mental health risk prediction. ADAPT uses variation in models estimated from previous calendar periods to characterize plausible changes in predictor-outcome relationships. Data from the current period constrain which historical patterns remain relevant, allowing the method to seek robustness against subsequent shifts while preserving contemporary discrimination. We retrospectively evaluated ADAPT using EHRs from 889,445 patients with mental health diagnoses at Mass General Brigham and Duke University Health System, covering one-year risk prediction for 28 outcomes. In the worst 20% of year-pair comparisons, ADAPT improved AUC over all comparators by 0.016-0.036 at Mass General Brigham, 0.011-0.018 at Duke, and 0.008-0.037 after transport. For suicide-attempt prediction, contemporary AUC at Mass General Brigham was 0.82 compared with 0.80 for the best comparator. Eight-year relative AUC degradation was 7.7%, compared with 12.1% for pooled-data training. These results suggest that information from prior temporal shifts can improve robustness to future changes without sacrificing predictive performance for current patients.

papers.title: Exploring the Attitudes, Barriers, Concerns, Differences, and Ethics (ABCDEs) of Healthcare Decision Making of Vagus Nerve Stimulation
papers.abstract: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) is an established neuromodulation therapy approved for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) and epilepsy, with growing interest in its application to other conditions. Despite demonstrated clinical efficacy, VNS remains underused in psychiatric care. This mixed-methods study examined stakeholder perceptions of VNS, focusing on access, stigma, ethical concerns, and acceptability across epilepsy, depression, heart failure (HF), and rheumatoid arthritis (RA). We conducted six focus groups and 20 semi-structured interviews with patients, clinicians, and one support person, and integrated qualitative themes with quantitative data on stigma and treatment barriers. Participants revealed stark disparities in VNS adoption: epilepsy patients reported fewer insurance barriers, while TRD participants faced delayed approvals, high out-of-pocket costs, and limited access to specialty care. Depression stakeholders reported higher stigma scores and expressed greater reluctance to consider surgical treatment, despite possessing comparable knowledge to epilepsy stakeholders. Ethical concerns, particularly regarding informed consent and impaired decision-making, surfaced frequently in the context of TRD. Most participants agreed that the appropriateness of VNS should align with disease severity and impact on quality of life. Many cautiously supported VNS for HF and RA, provided strong efficacy data supports its use. Hope emerged as a consistent theme, especially among TRD participants seeking alternatives after exhausting other treatments. These findings underscore the need to address insurance barriers, reduce stigma, and enhance provider education. As VNS expands into new indications, policymakers and clinicians must implement reforms that promote equitable access, decentralized care, and ethically sound consent practices to ensure inclusive neuromodulation therapy adoption.

papers.title: Core schema instability in youth at clinical high risk for psychosis: within-person variability as an index of self-belief precision
papers.abstract: Aim. Core schemas are considered stable traits in clinical high risk (CHR) research. However, unexamined fluctuation may conceal belief changes that precede psychosis emergence. We examined whether schemas possess considerable within-person variability in CHR, and whether that variability exceeds that of controls. Methods. In NAPLS 2, 411 CHR and 194 control participants completed the Brief Core Schema Scales (BCSS) at least three times across 24 months. Random-intercept models identified intraclass correlations in CHR. Bayesian censored location-scale models, correcting for floor scores and mean level differences, compared within-person SD between groups. Results. Within-person variance accounted for 41.3% to 50.6% of BCSS variance in CHR. Latent within-person SD was greater in CHR on all four subscales, most for negative-self (ratio 1.71, 95% CrI [1.50, 1.94]). This variability was largely independent of shared improvement and psychotropic medication effects. Conclusions. Core schemas fluctuate substantially in CHR compared to controls, particularly in negative self-beliefs. Single baseline scores may understate associations between schemas and outcomes.

papers.title: SPEECH FEATURES IN A DEVELOPMENTAL PERSPECTIVE: A SCREENING TOOL FOR PSYCHOSIS, DEPRESSION AND ANXIETY
papers.abstract: Language production provides a window into cognitive development, social cognition, and mental health. To translate this potential into clinical practice, we developed a scalable speech-based platform integrating graph-theoretical, psycholinguistic, and emotional features from brief spontaneous narratives to support developmental monitoring, mental wellness screening, and clinical decision-making. Normative developmental trajectories were derived from 2149 participants spanning 0-23 years of formal education. Narratives elicited using positively valenced pictures were transformed into word graphs to derive two composite indices: Narrative Complexity (NC), reflecting structural language organization, and Emotional Narrative Complexity (ENC), integrating narrative structure and emotional content. Both indices were modeled using asymptotic functions calibrated by schooling and converted into percentile-based normative curves. NC (R2 = 0.29, {tau} = 7.77) and ENC (R2 = 0.31, {tau} = 6.97) increased with schooling, approaching saturation around middle school. These trajectories provide educationally calibrated references for evaluating linguistic and socioemotional development. Clinical utility was investigated in a transdiagnostic sample of 120 participants, comprising healthy controls (n = 38), mood disorders (n = 28), affective psychosis (n = 36), and non-affective psychosis (n = 18). Although ENC alone did not discriminate between symptom-risk or diagnostic groups, classifiers combining its constituent variables with education and sex achieved AUCs of 0.726 for symptom risk and 0.800 for diagnosis, increasing to 0.774 and 0.858, respectively, with additional linguistic features. Machine-learning models integrating graph-derived, psycholinguistic, and emotional features further estimated symptom dimensions assessed by PANSS, GAD-7, and PHQ-9, achieving AUCs of 0.74-0.92 across severity thresholds while maintaining sensitivity [≥] 0.80. Individual linguistic variables also differed significantly across symptom-severity strata, suggesting distinct associations with psychopathological dimensions. Together, these findings establish an integrated speech-based framework spanning normative developmental assessment, mental wellness screening, and symptom-informed clinical support. By combining educationally calibrated trajectories with interpretable linguistic features and machine learning, this approach offers scalable digital markers to identify atypical developmental patterns, inform preventive strategies, and assist clinical assessment and decision-making.

papers.title: Pupil size-resting state network coupling in major depressive disorder: a longitudinal iTBS study
papers.abstract: Altered central-peripheral autonomic nervous system communication plays a key role in major depressive disorder (MDD). In this context, pupillary dynamics may be considered a non-invasive peripheral proxy of treatment-related changes during intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) in MDD. However, the relationship between spontaneous pupillary fluctuations and the resting-state functional networks (RSNs) involved in MDD is still underexplored. Here, we investigated longitudinal changes in pupil-RSN coupling in patients with MDD undergoing an iTBS intervention. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging with concurrent pupillometry was acquired at four study visits. Group independent component analysis was used to estimate tonic pupil coupling with predefined RSNs of interest, along with a linear mixed-effects model to assess longitudinal changes in pupil size-RSN coupling and, exploratively, the effect of potential clinical and behavioral moderators. Among the examined RSNs, the left executive control network (lECN), including the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex as the cortical target of stimulation, exhibited a sustained reduction in positive pupil size coupling relative to baseline, irrespective of treatment order (active-sham). To determine whether this longitudinal change was accompanied by a more general change in pupil diameter, we additionally examined pupil size independently of RSNs. Pupil diameter decreased significantly from baseline, with greater decreases being positively associated with greater reductions in anxiety scores. Notably, reduction in anxiety symptoms were also positively correlated with reduction in depressive symptoms. Together, these findings suggest that longitudinal reductions in pupil-IECN coupling occur alongside reductions in pupil diameter that are associated with reductions in anxiety symptoms.

papers.title: Synaptic density (SV2A) tracks illness chronicity rather than symptom severity in major depressive disorder
papers.abstract: Synaptic loss has been proposed as a key mechanism in major depressive disorder (MDD). Positron emission tomography with [11C]UCB-J enables in vivo quantification of synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A), a proxy marker of synaptic density. A landmark study by Holmes et al reported an inverse association between depression severity and SV2A binding in frontolimbic regions. As a replication, we examined this association in [11C]UCB-J PET data from 34 unmedicated individuals with MDD, focusing on the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and hippocampus. We found no support of an association between MADRS scores and SV2A binding in the primary regions of interest (r = 0.18-0.26, all p >= 0.15; 0.15). Findings were similar in unadjusted and age- and sex-adjusted models. However, adjustment for duration of the current depressive episode and lifetime depressive episodes yielded positive associations across primary regions. In post hoc analyses, longer current episode duration, but not lifetime depressive episodes, was negatively associated with SV2A binding across primary regions. Thus, our findings did not support an association between depression severity and synaptic density, contrary to a previous report; instead, the exploratory findings suggest that SV2A binding may be related to episode duration rather than current symptom burden.

papers.title: Psilocybin, cognitive stability and drinking reduction in co-occurring alcohol use disorder and depression: a pilot secondary analysis of a randomized, placebo-controlled trial
papers.abstract: Background. Change in cognitive control is a candidate transdiagnostic mechanism of psychedelic therapy. One account predicts that, once acute effects resolve, psilocybin shifts control toward flexibility while sparing inhibition and working memory. A motivational account (PRISM) predicts that psilocybin increases the willingness to exert control rather than the ability to do so. We tested both in patients with co-occurring alcohol use disorder (AUD) and major depression. Methods. In this secondary analysis of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of psilocybin for AUD with comorbid major depressive disorder (MDD; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04620759), a subset of participants (placebo n=13, psilocybin n=12) completed five cognitive tasks before drug administration and again about one week after it (mean 6.7 days, SD 1.1). Outcome measures spanned the stability-flexibility continuum. Free choice between levels of cognitive demand indexed the participant's willingness to exert control. Effect sizes and Bayes factors were used to estimate drug effects and associations with change in drinking and depressive symptoms across 34 retest measures. Results. Relative to placebo, psilocybin slowed responding in cued task switching (learning-phase RT d=1.01, BF10=7.7; switch trials d=1.12, BF10=17). Psilocybin effects on feedback-driven measures were inconsistent in direction (7 of 11 toward flexibility); the largest was on perseveration, which rose less with practice under psilocybin than under placebo (d=-0.79, BF10=1.1). Other drug effects on the 34 retest measures had inconclusive Bayes factors (BF10=0.40-2.4), and none survived false discovery rate correction. Demand avoidance, analyzed separately from the 34 measures, showed no detectable drug effect (BF01=2.0). Baseline demand avoidance showed no detectable relation to performance but tracked depressive symptoms (rho=.71, BF10=24). Drinking fell in both arms, and on 15 of 17 stability-flexibility measures change toward stability accompanied drinking reduction (stability composite rho=-.64, BF10=29; rho=-.43 when change was adjusted for baseline scores). Lower baseline working-memory span predicted larger drinking reductions (BF10=19-25). Depressive symptoms fell more after psilocybin than after placebo (PHQ-9, d=-0.88, BF10=2.7), but their change was not associated with cognitive change or predicted by working-memory span. Conclusions. About one week after dosing, psilocybin slowed cued task switching but had no consistent effect on feedback-driven flexibility, and there was no evidence of an effect on the willingness to exert effort. Drinking reduction was associated with increased, not reduced, cognitive stability, whereas improvement in depressive symptoms was not associated with cognitive change. These pilot estimates can guide adequately powered trials.

papers.title: Effect of food-cues on aMCC glutamate modulation during inhibitory control post weight loss intervention: a 1H fMRS study
papers.abstract: Objective: Poor inhibitory control may decrease weight loss maintenance. The neurobiological mechanisms are poorly understood. We investigated whether glutamate modulation in the anterior mid-cingulate cortex (aMCC) during response inhibition is impacted by food-cues and associated with self-reported behaviors and weight loss maintenance. Methods: 27 adults with overweight/obesity were recruited from a clinical weight management program. 1H fMRS (midline aMCC) was acquired during a visual-guided response inhibition task engaging two responding modes [non-selective (100% responses) or selective (withholding a response on 20% of trials)] applied with neutral (squares) or food/non-food cues. The impact of stimulus type on the aMCC glutamate modulation for each responding mode was assessed using a repeated measures GEE approach. Correlations were conducted between glutamate modulation, Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire scores, and long-term weight change. Results: The stimulus effect was significant during selective responding, driven by lower aMCC glutamate modulation during food/non-food cues. This glutamate modulation (selective; food/non-food) association with weight loss maintenance was a close trend (R2=0.15, p=0.054). The association with the TFEQ Cognitive Restraint was significant (R2=0.20, p=0.047). Conclusions: These results demonstrate an impact of food/non-food cues during response inhibition on the neurobiology and associations with long-term weight loss maintenance and scores related to eating behaviors.

papers.title: Post-psychedelic and meditation-related challenges: a protocol for a mixed-methods longitudinal-observational study
papers.abstract: Introduction: Psychedelics and meditation are increasingly used for therapeutic and wellness purposes. However, research into adverse effects (AEs) has been limited, without adequate investigation of the nature, clinical characteristics, and diversity of persisting challenges following psychedelic use and meditation practice. This study aims to better characterize the clinical and contextual features of these challenges, describe their longitudinal course, and compare psychedelic-related challenges to meditation-related challenges, selected as comparator conditions given previously characterized phenomenological and contextual overlap between the two. Methods and Analysis: This is a mixed-methods, enriched-sample, active-comparator (psychedelics vs. meditation) observational study comprising (1) a cross-sectional retrospective survey (N = 1,600), (2) a prospective 12-month longitudinal design involving six bimonthly surveys (n = 800), (3) 12 weeks of weekly ambulatory assessments combining quantitative symptom ratings with narrative voice report (n = 40), and (4) qualitative interviews (n = 60). Participants are recruited into two parallel arms of 800 each: individuals reporting psychedelic-related challenges and individuals reporting meditation-related challenges, defined as distress or impairment persisting after the acute effects of a psychedelic experience or period of meditation practice have subsided. Data collection includes a tailored item pool aimed at capturing the symptoms and phenomenology of these challenges in detail, developed from qualitative research and collaboratively with stakeholders with lived experience. The World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS 2.0) and measures of agent/exposure, set, setting, and social response are administered to characterize biopsychosocial correlates and functional impacts of AEs. Initial analyses will describe the phenomenology, course, and functional impact of psychedelic- and meditation-related challenges, and evaluate the structure and psychometric properties of the novel item pool. The study will produce a publicly available de-identified dataset supporting subsequent analyses, such as correspondence with recognized clinical syndromes, trajectory characterization, and cross-arm comparison of measurement structure, reported in registered reports or preregistrations.

papers.title: "It was like a weird, paralysing thing": Understanding the development and consequences of emotionally based school non-attendance (EBSNA) through young people's and parents' experiences.
papers.abstract: Emotionally based school non-attendance (EBSNA) is an increasing concern, yet relatively little research has integrated young people's and parents' perspectives to understand how attendance difficulties develop and affect young people and their families. This qualitative study explored the development and consequences of EBSNA through the complementary experiences of young people and parents. In-depth semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 parents and 16 young people aged 11-17 years who had experienced EBSNA. Young people could participate through either verbal or written interviews to support inclusive participation. Data were analysed using the Framework Method, with multiple researchers contributing to coding, charting and interpretation. Three overarching themes were identified: misalignment between young people's needs and the school environment; becoming unable to attend school; and the wider impact of EBSNA. Across accounts, EBSNA developed gradually through interactions between individual needs and school environments, rather than being attributable to individual characteristics alone. Sensory, social, organisational and academic demands, particularly during the transition to secondary school, combined with unmet needs, bullying, punitive practices and difficulties establishing trusting relationships to progressively undermine psychological safety and belonging. As distress escalated, anxiety increasingly extended beyond specific school situations to school itself, eventually making attendance feel psychologically and physically impossible. Once established, absence created additional barriers to returning through lost confidence, disrupted friendships and concerns about falling behind. Despite substantial educational disruption, young people generally remained motivated to learn. EBSNA also had profound social and family consequences, including isolation, deteriorating parental wellbeing, disrupted family relationships and financial pressures. Findings conceptualise EBSNA as a dynamic socioecological process and highlight the importance of early, individualised responses that address unmet needs and create psychologically safe, inclusive and supportive school environments.

papers.title: Childhood adverse experiences associate with reduced brain CB1 endocannabinoid receptor availability in healthy controls and patients with first-episode psychosis
papers.abstract: Background The brain endocannabinoid system (ECS) is dysregulated in first-episode psychosis (FEP) but understanding of the nature and origins of ECS dysregulation in FEP is limited. The imprinting of developmental adversity and stress into the adult ECS has not been previously studied in humans. We tested the hypothesis that childhood adverse events (ACE) associate with decreased brain type-1 endocannabinoid receptor (CB1R) availability in patients with FEP and healthy controls (HC). Methods CB1R availability was measured cross-sectionally in male and female patients with FEP (n=15), and healthy participants (n=20). Brain CB1R binding was measured with the selective CB1R radiotracer [18F]FMPEP-d2 using positron emission tomography (PET). Distribution volumes (VT) using metabolite corrected arterial input was a proxy of CB1R availability, which was measured in 13 functionally relevant regions of interest (ROI). ACE before the age of 16 were categorized as simple (0-1 events) or multiple ([≥] 2 events) using a Finnish population survey questionnaire. Results An rmANOVA model of regional CB1R VT (ROI ~ sex + group + sex*group + ACE) indicated statistically significant associations of ACE (p<0.001), group (p=0.027) and sex*group interaction(p=0.018). The largest effect sizes of ACE on CB1R were seen in the amygdala (2=.37), temporal cortex (2=.35), hippocampus (2=.33) and insula (2=.31). Discussion Multiple childhood adverse effects were associated with lower availability of temporo-limbic CB1R in adulthood in healthy participants and in patients with first-episode psychosis. These results corroborate previous results from pre-clinical studies, and expand the literature in showing that early adversity can be imprinted into the function of human brain in adulthood. The results have implications for studies on resilience and adaptation to stress as well as studies on vulnerability to psychiatric disorders.

papers.title: Feasibility and Preliminary Effects of a Culturally Adapted Internet-Based Mental Health Promotion Intervention for Indonesian Undergraduate Students (LifeHack: Menjadi Mahasiswa Tangguh): A Protocol for a Single-Arm, Pre-Post Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: Background: Mental health problems are highly prevalent among university students globally and in Indonesia, yet the vast majority do not receive adequate care. Whilst existing digital mental health interventions in Indonesia have primarily targeted students with clinically elevated symptoms, no prior study has evaluated an internet-based intervention designed to promote positive mental health among Indonesian university students. LifeHack is an internet-based guided self-help intervention developed to promote positive mental health as part of the Caring Universities initiative within the WHO World Mental Health-International College Student (WMH-ICS) framework. LifeHack: Menjadi Mahasiswa Tangguh is a culturally adapted Indonesian version, developed through a systematic adaptation process guided by Bernal's Ecological Validity Model and the Heuristic Framework for Cultural Adaptation. Objectives: This study aims to evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of the adapted intervention, including its usability, participant satisfaction, adherence, and retention. Secondarily, it will examine preliminary signals of change in resilience, positive mental health, depression and anxiety symptoms, and coping strategies. Methods: This protocol describes a single-arm pre-post feasibility study involving 50 undergraduate students aged 18-25 years from Universitas Padjadjaran and Universitas Jambi, Indonesia. Participants will receive the culturally adapted LifeHack: Menjadi Mahasiswa Tangguh, a self-paced web-based guided self-help intervention supported by asynchronous personalised feedback from trained e-coaches. Participants may select modules according to their individual needs and complete the intervention over a flexible period of 1-6 weeks. Assessments will be conducted at baseline (T0), immediately following intervention completion or at the end of the six-week intervention period if participants have not previously indicated completion (T1), and three months after T1 (T2). Primary feasibility outcomes include usability, satisfaction, intervention adherence, retention, and intervention completion. Secondary outcomes include resilience, positive mental health, psychological distress, coping, and safety. Safety will be assessed through participant-reported negative effects and recorded adverse events identified through routine e-coach monitoring. Progression to a future randomised controlled trial will be evaluated using pre-specified traffic light criteria. Expected Outcomes: Findings will inform the feasibility, cultural appropriateness, and preliminary effects of the adapted LifeHack intervention for Indonesian students. Results will guide potential progression to a fully powered randomised controlled trial.

papers.title: Negotiating belonging and identity across the life course: A qualitative study using Social Identity Mapping with people with psychosis
papers.abstract: A core part of how we understand ourselves comes from the groups we feel we belong to. Having positive, meaningful group memberships, or 'social identities', has been linked to better wellbeing in people diagnosed with psychotic disorders, yet little attention has been paid to how individuals with psychosis experience social identities and changes in belonging across the life course. Personal recovery in psychosis has been described as centred on identity and connection: it may be useful therefore to consider the experiences of people with psychosis from the perspective of the Social Identity Approach to Health (SIAH). This study used Social Identity Mapping (SIM) as the basis for semi-structured interviews (n = 28). Thematic analysis, conducted by a team drawing on wide-ranging expertise (lived experience, clinical psychiatry and social psychology), generated four themes: (1) Pre-symptom social identity conflict and non-belonging: 'I'm just something in-between'; (2) Psychosis tears identity apart: 'The map would have been blank'; (3) Social identification is both a risk and a requirement for recovery: 'Everyone wants to belong to some certain group or another'; and (4) Lack of identification with people with psychosis: 'Do I feel a part of that group? Not really, no'. This SIM-supported interview approach uncovered new insights into how people negotiate social identification before, during and after psychosis. Social identification may be a protective factor, and social identity-strengthening interventions should be evaluated as means of improving quality of life and social functioning.

papers.title: Familial factors inflate the estimated effects of genetic liability to ADHD on behavioural outcomes
papers.abstract: BackgroundPeople with ADHD have worse health, behavioural and social outcomes, widely interpreted as evidence that ADHD causes these harms, justifying early identification and treatment. But ADHD clusters in families, and conventional studies cannot separate the effect of a persons own ADHD from the family environment in which it arises. We used a family-based genetic design to distinguish the two. MethodsWe used up to 22 genome-wide significant variants associated with ADHD (38,691 cases, 186,843 controls) to estimate effects of genetic liability to ADHD on 16 health and behavioural outcomes. We compared population-based estimates with family-based estimates from within-sibship analyses of up to 164,220 siblings. We tested for heterogeneity between the designs, and applied sensitivity analyses. We involved individuals with lived experience of ADHD in interpreting the findings and shaping how the clinical/public-health implications were described. FindingsPopulation-based analyses implied that greater genetic liability to ADHD increased smoking, alcohol use and depressive symptoms, and reduced educational attainment, age at first child and cognitive performance. In family-based analyses, these effects attenuated. For example, the effect on number of depressive symptoms fell from 0{middle dot}059 SD (95% CI 0{middle dot}039, 0{middle dot}080) to 0{middle dot}002 SD (-0{middle dot}052, 0{middle dot}055), and age at first child increased from -0{middle dot}045 SD (-0{middle dot}058, -0{middle dot}033) to 0{middle dot}003 SD (-0{middle dot}040, 0{middle dot}047), with significant differences between designs (p=0{middle dot}048 and p=0{middle dot}034). Findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses. InterpretationMuch of the excess health and behavioural burden attributed to ADHD may reflect the family and environmental context in which ADHD occurs, rather than an individuals own ADHD. Interventions targeting the individual might not reduce these outcomes as much as expected. Distinguishing such effects requires family-based designs. FundingMedical Research Council, UK Research and Innovation, Research Council of Norway, US National Institute of Mental Health, and Australian National Health and Medical Research Council. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSAttention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and higher genetic liability to ADHD, are associated with a wide range of adverse health, behavioural, and social outcomes. A 2024 umbrella review of the impacts of ADHD summarised consistent associations with addiction, mental and physical illness, lower educational attainment, and social difficulties. Earlier reviews of Mendelian randomization studies of ADHD reached similar conclusions, reporting apparent causal effects on smoking, depression, body-mass index, and educational attainment. A broad two-sample Mendelian randomization analysis of ADHD across more than 100 traits corroborated these findings. Almost all of this genetic evidence, however, comes from samples of unrelated individuals, in which estimates can be confounded by population stratification, assortative mating, and dynastic effects. We searched PubMed and Google Scholar from database inception to 20/07/26 using terms related to ADHD, Mendelian randomization, and within-family designs (Supplementary note), without language restrictions. We identified eight relevant studies, however only three used a within-family or trio Mendelian randomization design. None used a large within-family Mendelian randomization design to investigate the effects of genetic liability to ADHD on health or behavioural outcomes while separating individuals liability from familial influences. Added value of this studyTo our knowledge, this is the largest within-family Mendelian randomization study of genetic liability to ADHD, comparing conventional population-based estimates with family-based estimates across 16 outcomes in up to 164,220 siblings. Population-based estimates reproduced previously reported associations, but most attenuated in family-based analyses. For depressive symptoms and age at first child, the two designs significantly differed, indicating that the population-based estimates were inflated by familial factors. Implications of all the available evidenceMuch of the excess health, behavioural, and social burden attributed to ADHD may reflect the family and environmental context in which ADHD arises, rather than an individuals own liability. If so, interventions directed solely at the individual may not reduce these outcomes as much as observational and population-based estimates imply. These findings should be interpreted alongside the broader evidence rather than as a basis for immediate changes in practice, and they underscore the need for larger family-based genetic studies.

papers.title: Interoceptive mechanisms of body image disturbance in anorexia nervosa: Study protocol of a randomized parallel-group trial
papers.abstract: BackgroundCurrent treatments for anorexia nervosa (AN), a dangerous psychiatric disorder, show only moderate efficacy. Interoceptive processing dysfunctions (i.e., how the brain receives and processes body afferents), and body image disturbance (BID) are clinical features of AN. Floatation-REST (Reduced Environmental Stimulation Therapy) has been reported to enhance both subjective interoceptive experiences and BID. The proposed project works to establish (1) how interoceptive processing dysfunctions may contribute to BID and (2) how the combination of Floatation-REST with psychotherapeutic principles may enhance interoceptive processing and BID in AN. MethodsIn this randomized parallel-group (NCT06332963), single-site trial, 102 women and girls with AN will be recruited from an inpatient program. After completing baseline measurements, participants are randomized on a 1:1 ratio to receive either the interoceptively focused treatment (IFT) or exteroceptively focused treatment (EFT) condition. Both conditions utilize acceptance- and mindfulness-based principles, however incorporate skills that focus on interoception or exteroception, respectively. Participants complete acute measures following each experimental therapeutic session, as well as post intervention, six-week and six-month follow-up. The primary outcome of the current study is acute changes in BID assessed by the Photographic Figure Rating Scale. Additional outcomes include acute changes in interoception, and longitudinal intervention effects on self-reported, behavioral, and neuroimaging measures of AN symptoms, BID, and interoception. DiscussionIf interventions demonstrate reductions in BID, mechanisms of BID will be further understood, informing the development of future therapies for BID in AN.

papers.title: Structural brain network organization and aggressive behavior in schizophrenia: a mega-analysis of 2260 patients and 3058 healthy controls from the ENIGMA-Schizophrenia Working Group
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlthough most individuals with schizophrenia do not show aggressive behavior, rates are higher than in the general population. Identifying the neurobiological correlates of aggression may inform prevention. MethodsWe included 2260 individuals with schizophrenia spectrum disorders and 3058 healthy controls (HC) from 26 sites in the ENIGMA-Schizophrenia Working Group. The former were classified as showing at least moderate aggression (SZ+A; N = 231) or not (SZ-A; N = 2029) based on symptom rating scales. Structural covariance networks were constructed from cortical and subcortical volumes. We examined global and nodal network topology, as well as density within six large-scale brain networks and between each network and the rest of the brain. Metrics were summarized as the area under the curve (AUC) across a prespecified range of densities (K = 0.10-0.25, {Delta}K = 0.01). Group differences were assessed using pairwise permutation tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. ResultsGlobal and nodal network topology did not differ significantly between SZ+A and HC. Network-rest density of the salience network (SN) was higher in SZ+A than in HC, although this difference did not survive multiple-comparison correction ({Delta}AUC = 0.018, pBH = .083). In exploratory subgroup analyses, higher SN network-rest density was observed only in SZ+A with high delusion severity ({Delta}AUC = 0.021, p = .007). By contrast, SZ-A demonstrated extensive alterations in global network topology compared with SZ+A and HC, alongside selective alterations in nodal topology and large-scale network density compared with HC. Results were broadly consistent across sensitivity analyses using alternative definitions of aggression and adjusting for current antipsychotic dose. ConclusionsSZ+A was characterized by fewer--not more--abnormalities in structural covariance network organization than SZ-A, which may reflect etiological heterogeneity. In SZ+A with high delusion severity, higher network-rest density of the SN may point to aberrant salience processing in aggressive behavior.

papers.title: Simulating Psychotherapeutic Sessions with Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Proof-of-Concept Study of In Silico Psychotherapy Research
papers.abstract: BackgroundAcross biomedicine, in silico models increasingly complement in vivo and in vitro research. Psychotherapy science, however, remains constrained by methodological limitations, resource-intensive trials, challenges in manipulating clinically meaningful features experimentally, and a potential ceiling in efficacy. Leveraging generative AI and large language models (LLMs), we propose a framework for "in silico psychotherapy research": controlled simulations of psychotherapeutic interactions under reproducible experimental conditions. ObjectiveWe test whether such simulation experiments can recover a theoretically expected effect of an isolated psychotherapy-process manipulation. MethodsIn a preregistered proof-of-concept study, we generated 512 fully automated motivational interviewing (MI) sessions by linking locally deployed Llama-3.3-70B-In-struct based therapist and patient models across eight vignettes and eight therapist personas. Therapist, but not patient, prompts manipulated common therapeutic factors (CTF), contrasting high versus low empathy, affirmation, and alliance building behaviour in a controlled design. The primary outcome was MI treatment integrity (MITI 4.2 global ratings), assessed by a blinded LLM with repeated ratings and analysed using linear mixed-effects models. Secondary outcomes included observer-inferred importance/confidence rulers based on simulated patient utterances; Therapist Empathy Scale (TES) and Working Alliance Inventory-Short Observer (WAI-S-O) served as manipulation fidelity checks. Human coders rated a stratified subsample. ResultsOf the 512 simulations, 506 (98.8%) yielded complete transcripts and 480 (93.75) were retained for analysis. Manipulation checks confirmed the fidelity of the CTF manipulation (WAI-S-O total scores {beta}=3.14; [2.65,3.63], p<0.001, TES {beta}=14.48 [13.92,15.04], p<0.001). High versus low CTF produced a theoretically expected improvement in all MITI global ratings, including the MI-specific features not directly targeted by the CTF manipulation ({beta}=0.54-0.95; all p<0.001). Simulated patient confidence but not importance for change increased more under high CTF ({beta}=0.17 [0.09,0.26], p<0.001). Human ratings confirmed the direction of the primary contrast. ConclusionsLLM-based psychotherapy simulations were technically feasible, demonstrated experimental fidelity, and showed theoretically concordant effects beyond directly manipulated constructs and simulation participants. These findings provide proof of concept for in silico psychotherapy research as a promising complementary pre-clinical experimental paradigm for hypothesis generation and testing to support accelerated intervention development. The applicability of this approach across patient populations, therapeutic modalities and model architectures requires further evaluation. Trial Pre-registrationClinicalTrials.gov NCT06813066; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06813066?term=NCT06813066

papers.title: Polygenic liability for major depression, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder and treatment outcome across major psychiatric disorders
papers.abstract: Polygenic scores for major depression, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder have been related to treatment outcome. We analysed 4,007 patients of European ancestry from 7 cohorts: three with major depression (STAR*D, GSRD, PANDORA), two with bipolar disorder (STEP-BD, Barcelona) and two with schizophrenia (CATIE, HSRRm). The three scores were computed with PRS-CS from the latest Psychiatric Genomics Consortium studies. The primary outcome was good response or good course, harmonized from each cohorts instrument. Firth logistic regression within cohorts, adjusted for age, sex and ancestry components, was followed by random-effects pooling. A higher depression score was associated with lower odds of a good outcome (odds ratio per standard deviation 0.88, 95% confidence interval 0.79-0.99, p = .04; false discovery rate q = .11). The estimate remained below one in all 8 sensitivity analyses, including adjustment for baseline severity, and was negative in all 5 cohorts with a continuous improvement measure. The schizophrenia score pointed the same way (odds ratio 0.93, 95% confidence interval 0.85-1.01) with no heterogeneity. The bipolar score showed no pooled effect (odds ratio 0.97), and its direction differed by diagnosis. In pooled data spanning three diagnoses, higher polygenic liability to depression was nominally associated with a less favourable treatment outcome, although the association did not survive correction for multiple testing; schizophrenia liability showed a similar directional trend. These findings support further evaluation of disorder liability in multivariable models of treatment outcome.

papers.title: Systematic evaluation of semantic similarity across language models for schizophrenia spectrum disorders
papers.abstract: BackgroundSemantic similarity features derived from language embeddings have been proposed as markers of schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD), but prior studies have reported inconsistent directions of effect and limited evidence regarding their relationship to specific dimensions of thought and language disturbance. We systematically evaluated how language model architecture and preprocessing strategy influence semantic similarity signals in SSD. MethodsSpeech samples from 228 participants (152 SSD, 76 healthy volunteers) were analyzed using six embedding models: GloVe, LSA, Word2Vec, RoBERTa, GPT-2, and Llama. Semantic similarity features were computed across three preprocessing levels (verbatim, disfluency-removed, and disfluency-removed with stopword filtering) using k-interword, moving-window, and sentence-to-sentence comparisons, summarized with various statistical descriptors. Features were compared between SSD and healthy volunteers and examined for associations with dimensions of thought and language disturbance, including inefficiency, incoherence, and impaired expressivity. ResultsSSD was predominantly associated with increased semantic similarity across models and comparison strategies. Model performance varied by preprocessing. RoBERTa performed best on minimally processed transcripts, yielding the greatest number of diagnosis-associated features, whereas GPT-2 achieved the largest diagnostic effect size after maximal preprocessing. GPT-2 showed the strongest signal for inefficiency and incoherence, while RoBERTa yielded the greatest number of associations with impaired expressivity. ConclusionsSSD diagnosis and its dimensions of thought and language abnormalities are characterized primarily by greater semantic proximity in open-ended speech. Optimal preprocessing depends on model architecture and the clinical dimension of interest, highlighting the importance of model-and phenotype-specific analytic choices in computational studies of thought and language disturbance in SSD.

papers.title: Multimodal Prediction of Distressing and Persistent Psychotic-Like Experiences in Adolescence across Environment, Genetics, and Neuroimaging
papers.abstract: Adolescent psychotic-like experiences, particularly those that are distressing and persistent (dpPLEs), may elevate risk for a range of psychiatric disorders, yet the relative predictive contributions of brain structure, genetics, and environment to dpPLEs remain unknown. Using four timepoints from 7,399 children in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, we developed stacked ensemble machine-learning models integrating cortical morphometry and whole-brain microstructural properties, polygenic risk scores, family psychiatric history, and childhood environmental factors to predict adolescent dpPLEs. Environmental predictors alone, driven by area deprivation index, neighborhood drug-related crime, and cumulative early adversity, were the strongest predictive domain (ROC-AUC = 0.687 {+/-} 0.003), outperforming genetic (0.619 {+/-} 0.020) and all imaging models (0.588-0.650). Adding genetic risk to environmental features produced the best-performing model overall (ROC-AUC = 0.697 {+/-} 0.007), whereas adding neuroimaging yielded no further incremental gain (ROC-AUC=0.683-0.696). Beyond environmental exposures, family history of psychosis, cross-disorder polygenic risk, and both globally distributed and regionally specific imaging components contributed to prediction. Childhood environmental factors thus capture a core predictive signal preceding dpPLEs, while genetic and neuroimaging features added comparatively modest discriminative prediction value, but may offer complementary biological insights.

papers.title: Posterior-anterior striatal reorganization after weight restoration in anorexia nervosa is associated with remission outcome: from mice to longitudinal human study
papers.abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe psychiatric disorder with high relapse rates despite successful weight restoration. Altered reward processing and an imbalance between goal-directed and habitual control within the striatum have been proposed to contribute to the persistence of maladaptive behaviours, but the striatal mechanisms underlying recovery and relapse remain unclear. Here, we combined cross-species structural MRI, including cross-sectional analyses in mice and longitudinal neuroimaging and clinical assessments in patients with AN, to investigate striatal alterations associated with recovery. Male mice with deletion of the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChTcKO; n = 9), a model of maladaptive eating behaviour, showed reduced dorsolateral striatal volume compared with wild-type mice (n=9). At baseline, women with AN (n = 71) showed reduced striatal volumes compared with healthy controls (n = 30). Longitudinally, patients with AN (n = 41) and healthy controls (n = 28) were reassessed, revealing substantial recovery of striatal volumes following weight restoration in AN. Posterior-anterior putamen gradient changes differed according to subsequent remission status, with changes in the right putamen gradient predicting relapse. Striatal gradient changes were also associated with goal-directed and habitual behaviour during the slip-of-action task, response consistency during delay discounting, and circulating ghrelin and desacyl ghrelin concentrations. These findings identify longitudinal putamen reorganization as a candidate marker of vulnerability to relapse and link striatal plasticity, goal-directed and habitual control, reward processing, and metabolic processes in AN.

papers.title: Ecological momentary assessment of anxiety and depression in individuals with early-treated phenylketonuria
papers.abstract: BackgroundIn addition to cognitive difficulties, individuals with early-treated phenylketonuria (PKU) may be at increased risk for anxiety and depression. However, previous findings are mixed, potentially due to reliance on retrospective self-report measures that are vulnerable to recall bias and lose resolution of day-to-day symptom fluctuations. The present study used ecological momentary assessment (EMA) to evaluate anxiety and depressive symptoms in adults with PKU in real-world settings. MethodsA sample of 30 adults with early-treated PKU and a demographically-similar sample of 30 adults without PKU completed smartphone-based EMA assessments four times daily over seven consecutive days (nTotal=1,384). Anxiety and depression symptoms and processing speed task performance were assessed at each timepoint. Previous week retrospective measures of mood symptoms were also collected following the EMA period. ResultsEMA compliance was high (82.4%). Momentary analyses revealed that PKU participants reported significantly greater anxiety and depression symptoms as well as poorer processing speed performance compared to healthy controls. In contrast, no significant group differences were identified using retrospective mood measures. Within the PKU group, Phe levels were not significantly associated with mood symptom severity or processing speed. ConclusionsEMA detected PKU-related differences in psychological symptoms that were not identified by traditional retrospective assessments. These findings highlight the feasibility and sensitivity of EMA for characterizing everyday functioning in individuals with PKU. EMA may provide a more accurate assessment of symptom burden and may be particularly valuable for studying rare clinical populations, where intensive longitudinal data collection can maximize information gained from relatively small samples. HighlightsO_LIEMA detected PKU-related elevations in anxiety and depression symptoms C_LIO_LIGroup differences were not evident on retrospective mood measurement C_LIO_LIEMA may be particularly valuable for studying rare clinical populations like PKU C_LI

papers.title: Cumulative Prenatal Adversity and Fronto-Limbic White Matter Development Across Adolescence
papers.abstract: ImportanceThe prenatal period is a critical window for intergenerational transmission of adversity, yet the neural substrates through which cumulative prenatal stress becomes biologically embedded in offspring brain development remain poorly understood. White matter microstructure is a candidate mechanism linking prenatal adversity to downstream emotional dysregulation. ObjectiveTo examine associations between cumulative adverse prenatal exposure (APE) burden and fronto-limbic white matter fractional anisotropy (FA) at baseline and across adolescent developmental trajectories, and to test whether white matter FA mediates prenatal APE effects on emotional dysregulation. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsCohort study using data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, Release 7.0, a diverse longitudinal cohort of US children recruited at ages 9 to 10 years across 21 sites. After diffusion tensor imaging quality control exclusions and retention of one twin or triplet per family, the final cross-sectional analytic sample comprised 10 483 participants. Longitudinal analyses included participants with data at one or more follow-up timepoints across four imaging waves. ExposuresCumulative APE burden, operationalized as a sum of six binary adverse prenatal exposures (unplanned pregnancy; early alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis use before pregnancy recognition; complicated pregnancy; complicated birth; range, 0-6) following Zhi et al. (2026). Main Outcomes and MeasuresFractional anisotropy in 11 a priori fronto-limbic white matter tracts at baseline (ages approximately 10 years) and across four imaging timepoints (ages approximately 10, 12, 14, and 16 years). Exploratory outcomes included Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) dysregulation profile and Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ) subscales. ResultsHigher prenatal APE burden was associated with lower baseline FA in left uncinate fasciculus (b = -0.00096; 95% CI, -0.00151 to -0.00042; FDR-corrected P = .006), corpus callosum (b = -0.00079; 95% CI, -0.00125 to -0.00032; FDR-corrected P = .006), and right uncinate fasciculus (b = -0.00071; 95% CI, -0.00120 to -0.00021; FDR-corrected P = .019). This association was stable across visits and robust to stringent adjustment for two complementary image-quality metrics (framewise displacement and frame censoring); prenatal burden was itself unassociated with image quality. Higher APE burden was additionally associated with steeper FA increases across adolescence (positive APE x Age interaction in 5 of 11 tracts); positive across all 11), these trajectory effects were more sensitive to image quality, though the right uncinate fasciculus association survived stringent adjustment. Post hoc analyses indicated that pregnancy complications and prenatal cannabis exposure were the most consistent contributors. White matter FA partially mediated the association between prenatal APE burden and involuntary emotional dysregulation, with no association with voluntary emotion regulation strategies. Conclusions and RelevanceCumulative prenatal APE burden was associated with lower fronto-limbic white matter FA --particularly in the uncinate fasciculus and corpus callosum--an enduring association that was stable across adolescence and robust to rigorous image-quality adjustment. Evidence for altered developmental trajectories was more sensitive to image quality and should be interpreted as a more tentative, complementary finding. These findings identify fronto-limbic white matter as a candidate neurobiological correlate of cumulative prenatal adversity, while underscoring that this pathway reflects a bounded set of prenatal exposures. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSIs cumulative adverse prenatal exposure burden associated with fronto-limbic white matter microstructure across adolescence? FindingsIn this cohort study of 10 483 adolescents from the ABCD Study, higher adverse prenatal exposure burden was associated with lower fractional anisotropy in bilateral uncinate fasciculus and corpus callosum --a stable association across adolescence that was robust to rigorous image-quality adjustment. Higher burden was additionally associated with steeper fractional anisotropy increases in 5 of 11 tracts, and white matter partially mediated associations with involuntary emotional dysregulation. MeaningThese findings identify fronto-limbic white matter microstructure as a candidate neurobiological correlate of cumulative prenatal adversity, consistent with early biological embedding through prenatal programming.

papers.title: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction for Generalized Anxiety Disorder: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the efficacy and safety of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) for anxiety symptoms in adults with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). DesignSystematic review and meta-analysis. Data SourcesCINAHL, Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Scopus, SocINDEX, ERIC (EBSCO), and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global were searched from inception to October 2025; identified trial protocols were hand-searched for subsequent reports through February 2026. Eligibility criteria for selecting studiesRandomized, non-randomized, and single-arm trials evaluating the effects of MBSR on anxiety in adults with GAD. Data extraction and synthesisTwo authors independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. The primary outcome was anxiety symptoms; the secondary outcome was adverse events. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted, and certainty of evidence was assessed. ResultsOf 19 included reports (16 independent samples), 8 randomized controlled trials (n=1,012) were included in the primary meta-analysis. MBSR significantly reduced anxiety symptoms vs. waitlist (Hedges g=-0.88; 95% CI -1.57 to -0.19) and general active comparators (g=-0.85; 95% CI -1.15 to -0.54), and showed no significant difference vs. escitalopram in two linked trials (g=0.09; 95% CI -0.11 to 0.29), with fewer adverse events in the in-person trial, the only one reporting them (15% vs. 79%; number needed to treat to avoid harm=2). GRADE certainty of evidence was high for the escitalopram comparison and very low for waitlist. ConclusionsMBSR is a well-tolerated, nonpharmacologic treatment option for adults with GAD. Anxiety reductions were similar to escitalopram, with fewer adverse events; independent replication is needed. MBSR may be a viable option for patients who prefer non-pharmacological management or who cannot tolerate medication. Systematic review registrationPROSPERO CRD420251140213. SUMMARY BOXO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSO_LIGeneralized anxiety disorder (GAD) is common and disabling, and pharmacotherapy is frequently discontinued because of adverse effects C_LIO_LIPrevious reviews of mindfulness-based interventions for anxiety pooled different programs and diagnoses, with inconsistent findings C_LIO_LIRecent noninferiority trials comparing Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) with escitalopram had not been synthesized C_LI What this study addsO_LIMBSR reduced anxiety symptoms compared with waitlist and general active comparators, although certainty of evidence for the waitlist comparison was very low C_LIO_LIIn two linked trials, anxiety reductions with MBSR were similar to those with escitalopram (high certainty evidence; g=0.09, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.29), with fewer adverse events in the in-person trial (15% v 79%; number needed to treat to avoid harm 2) C_LIO_LIIndependent replication and head-to-head trials against cognitive behavioral therapy are needed C_LI

papers.title: Early-Life Environmental Exposures and Brain Structure in Schizophrenia
papers.abstract: BackgroundSchizophrenia is widely considered a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by premorbid alterations in brain structure. Urban upbringing is a well-established environmental risk factor. However, urbanicity is often operationalised using broad population-based measures, leaving unclear which features of urban environments might affect the developing brain. This gap limits progress in understanding the pathways linking urban upbringing to schizophrenia, an increasingly important question as global urbanisation progresses. Cortical gyrification is especially informative in this context, as it is largely established before birth and remains relatively stable thereafter, offering a promising retrospective marker of early-life neurodevelopmental disturbances. Study DesignIn this case-control MRI study, we examined whether residential environmental exposures at birth were associated with adult brain structure in 51 individuals with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and 88 healthy controls matched for age, sex and socioeconomic status. Birth addresses were linked to geospatial measures of air pollution, green space, built volume, built surface and population density. Study ResultsHigher air pollution at birth was associated with lower cortical gyrification in individuals with schizophrenia, but not in healthy controls, particularly in orbitofrontal and inferior frontal regions. No comparable associations were observed for grey matter volume, cortical thickness or surface area. ConclusionsThese findings suggest that air pollution at birth may be linked to hypogyria in schizophrenia and provide a potential bridge between epidemiological research on urbanicity and neurodevelopmental models of schizophrenia. In turn, this work provides a critical starting point for future work assessing how early urban environments become biologically embedded in schizophrenia risk.

papers.title: Protocol for: Diagnostic trajectories of patients receiving unspecified psychosis-spectrum diagnoses. A retrospective, longitudinal, register-based study in a large UK secondary mental healthcare service from 2007 to 2024
papers.abstract: BackgroundUnspecified psychosis-spectrum diagnoses (ICD code F29) are commonly used when the underlying disorder remains uncertain, particularly at first presentation. These diagnoses may persist or later be revised as the clinical picture evolves, yet little is known about their long-term trajectories or implications for treatment and service use in routine mental healthcare. ObjectivesTo describe the usage and persistence of unspecified non-organic psychosis (F29) and other non-specific diagnoses, and the time to transition to a specific diagnosis. Secondary objectives are to describe temporal trends in their use, identify demographic and clinical characteristics associated with diagnostic persistence, and characterise treatment patterns, service utilisation, mortality, and discharge across diagnostic groups. MethodsWe will conduct a retrospective longitudinal cohort study using de-identified electronic health-record data from the South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust (SLaM), accessed through the Clinical Record Interactive Search (CRIS) system, between 1 January 2007 and 31 December 2024. The study population will include patients with an ICD-10 psychosis-spectrum diagnosis (F2x.x), substance induced psychotic disorder (or F1x.5), bipolar disorder or affective disorder with documented psychotic symptoms(F32/3.3). Diagnoses will be classified as specific or non-specific according to their ICD-10 category. Primary analysis will examine time from first F29 diagnosis to first subsequent specific psychosis-spectrum or bipolar diagnosis using Cox proportional hazards regression, with discharge from SLaM, death and administrative end of follow-up treated as censoring events. Associations with diagnostic transition will be examined adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, area-level deprivation, route of service entry, and calendar period. Secondary competing-risk analysis will estimate the cumulative incidence of diagnostic transition using the Aalen- Johansen estimator, treating discharge and death as competing events. Ethics and DisseminationCRIS operates under ethical approval from the South Central-Oxford C Research Ethics Committee (23/SC/0257). Project-specific approval was received from the CRIS Oversight Committee as Project 23-095. The study will be reported in accordance with the RECORD extension of the STROBE guidelines. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication and will provide evidence on the longitudinal use and refinement of non-specific psychosis-spectrum diagnoses in routine secondary mental healthcare.

papers.title: Developmental trajectories of child resilience, their determinants, and associations with risk experiences and behaviours: protocol for a national cohort study within the ReDiKid project
papers.abstract: BackgroundResilience during the transition from middle childhood towards early adolescence is best understood as a dynamic, adversity-activated developmental process rather than a fixed individual trait. Building on the Resilient Kid in the Digital World framework, this protocol describes the longitudinal component of the broader research programme, designed to characterise developmental trajectories of resilience-related capacities and resources and adaptive functioning, identify their determinants, and examine prospective associations with risk experiences and behaviours across behavioural, family, school, and digital contexts. MethodsThis is a national school-based cohort study following children aged 9-11 years at baseline across four waves at approximately six-month intervals from autumn 2025 to spring 2027. Schools are selected from the Czech national register using stratified probability-proportional-to-size sampling by region, municipality status, and area-level socioeconomic status; all eligible Grade 4 and Grade 5 pupils in participating schools are invited. The recruitment plan covers approximately 72 schools and 8,000 eligible children, with an anticipated 50-60% participation rate for complete child-parent pairs, corresponding to a target of approximately 4,000-4,800 linked child-parent dyads at baseline. Longitudinal planning aims to retain at least 1,000 linked dyads through Wave 4. Data are collected through child self-report, parent self- and proxy-report, and school-coordinator online questionnaires. Measures cover resilience-related capacities and resources, adaptive functioning and well-being, risk exposures, digital engagement, health-related behaviours, family context, parental mediation, and school context. Analyses will be tailored to the specific research questions and may include longitudinal and multilevel approaches complemented by reciprocal and person-oriented analyses. DiscussionThe study provides a multi-dimensional, nationally distributed longitudinal resource for examining how child functioning and resilience-related resources change together with risk experiences and contextual conditions during a key developmental transition. The design explicitly distinguishes resilience-related measures from evidence of resilience under adversity and treats digital environments as one interacting developmental context rather than as an isolated exposure domain. The cohort may also inform understanding of early vulnerability and protective processes relevant to problematic digital engagement, without treating such indicators as clinical diagnoses.

papers.title: Prevalence of DSM-5 eating disorders and associated impairment and service use among children and young people in England: analysis of a general population survey
papers.abstract: BackgroundEating disorders (EDs) typically emerge in adolescence and carry substantial morbidity. DSM-5 revised EDs classification, introducing Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder (OSFED) and Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID). We estimated general population prevalence of EDs, including ARFID, in children and young people (CYP), and the associated impairment, which remains poorly characterised. MethodsWe analysed the Mental Health of Children and Young People in England (MHCYP) 2023 survey, a nationally representative probability sample. All participants were screened for possible eating problems. Screen positives and a random sample of screen negatives were invited to a second-stage assessment; giving an analytic sample of 1,738 aged 11-25 years. Associations with impairment, mental health difficulties and service use were estimated using survey-weighted regression adjusted for age and sex. ResultsAny ED affected 6.7% (95% CI 5.4-8.3) of 11-25-year-olds and was over three times more common in females (10.7%) than males (3.0%). OSFED was the commonest (3.5%), followed by bulimia nervosa (1.7%), anorexia nervosa (0.9%), binge eating disorder (0.6%) and ARFID (0.2%). Prevalence peaked at 17-19 years (13.9%). EDs were associated with lifetime self-harm (aOR 9.1 at 11-16; 4.4 at 17-25), SDQ-predicted probable disorder (aOR 14.7; 2.5), medication use (aOR 5.3) and mental health service contact (aOR 2.1). ConclusionsEDs are common among CYP in England and carry high levels of impairment, self-harm and comorbid mental health difficulties, particularly among 11-16-year-olds. Nonetheless, more than half of those meeting diagnostic criteria had no mental health service contact in the preceding year.

papers.title: Self-harm incidents and restrictive practice use in an acute female inpatient unit: a service evaluation of a continuous multi-system improvement approach
papers.abstract: BackgroundSelf-harm is a frequent and challenging occurrence in adult inpatient psychiatric units. The use of restrictive practice to manage self-harm incidents continues to be widespread within mental health environments despite increasing national and organisational guidance to minimise its use. Purpose/aimThe aim of this project was to introduce and evaluate a continuous quality improvement programme to progressively reduce incidents of self-harm and the use of restrictive practice. The project was set in a female acute mental health inpatient unit. The project sought to embed improvements in an inpatient units interventions, procedures, and culture and staffs mindset, and move towards a sustained collaborative and positive therapeutic and communication-based approach. MethodsA retrospective service evaluation design was employed to assess differences in the number of incidents of self-harm, enhanced observation, seclusion, restraint and rapid tranquillisation in the period following the introduction of a continuous whole-systems multimodal interventional initiative in 2019. Pre- and post-initiation data were compared (2017/18 compared to 2019/2025) to evaluate improvement and whether this had been sustained. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, and means. ResultsSelf-harm incidents reduced between 2017/18 and 2019, with a downward trend sustained between 2019 and 2025 (136 to 72 incidents respectively between 2019 and 2025; 47% reduction). A sustained reduction in the use of restrictive practice was shown in all domains pre- and post-initiation (2017/18 compared to 2025). Clinical implicationsNo one approach will successfully reduce self-harm and the use of restrictive practice. Approaches employed have to be multi-faceted, multi-interdisciplinary, collaborative, and blend together to deliver improvement. Sustained progress requires commitment to an iterative process of continuous collaboration, improvement and adaptation.

papers.title: Autistic Adults' Perceptions of the Adequacy of their Supports and Disability-Related Information: Instrument Validation & Preliminary Correlates
papers.abstract: Autistic adults face considerable challenges in receiving adequate support, from both paid/formal (such as from disability services) and unpaid/informal (for example, from friends and family) sources. Having adequate support can lead to better health and well-being outcomes. However, most instruments designed to assess adequacy of support were not made specifically for/with autistic adults. This paper presents a psychometric validation of the AASPIRE Adequacy of Supports and Information Scale (AASIS), a community-informed adaptation of a previously developed instrument (the Quality of Care and Support scale; Lucas-Carrasco et al., 2011), designed to be relevant and accessible to autistic adults. We also used the AASIS to explore correlates of perceptions of support in a sample of 798 autistic adults. Our confirmatory factor analysis supported a two-factor structure for the AASIS (factor one: Supports; factor two: Information). Further testing confirmed the instrument was invariant across several groups, including race/ethnicity, gender, intellectual disability, communication fluency, and self-versus proxy-report. Regression analyses suggested that the way in which participants joined the study (i.e., through community advertisements or via established healthcare/disability services) impacted whether they viewed their support as adequate. Additionally, a higher number of adverse childhood events and greater experience of discrimination were related to worse perceptions of support adequacy across both factors. Our findings support the preliminary validity of the AASIS across a variety of autistic people, though further testing is warranted. Findings also point to the importance of addressing the needs of autistic people who are minoritized and/or who have complex trauma histories.
